newsitem.title: USA: Clinton routs Dole but Republicans hold Congress.
newsitem.headline: Clinton routs Dole but Republicans hold Congress.

text.p: Democratic President Bill Clinton routed Republican Bob Dole on Tuesday to win a sweet re-election triumph, but it appeared the voters would also put a check on Clinton by keeping Congress Republican.

Computerized voter tallies by television networks projected Clinton the winner in at least 30 of the 50 U.S. states to only 15 for Dole, as voting neared its conclusion at 11 p.m. EST (0400 GMT Wednesday).

That gave Clinton -- a man discounted by many as a one-term lame-duck only two years ago at the low point of his presidency -- 367 Electoral College votes to 132 for Dole. That was 97 more than the 270 needed to win under the indirect presidential voting system.

Dole, 73, the former Senate majority leader from Kansas and consummate Washington power-broker, conceded graciously, telling flag-waving, chanting supporters in Washington he had congratulated Clinton by phone.

He added: "I was just thinking in the elevator on my way downstairs, tomorrow will be the first time in my life i dont have anything to do." His eyes misted a bit as the crowd chanted, "Thank you, Bob! Thank you, Bob!" and he silenced them when they began jeering at Clinton's name.

Clinton, 50, the first president from the post-war "baby boom" generation, also became the first Democrat re-elected since Franklin Roosevelt in 1944 -- two years before Clinton was born, and when Dole was toting a rifle as a World War II infantryman.

He acknowledged victory before his own throng of exultant supporters in his home town of Little Rock, standing on the white columned steps of the old Arkansas capital building with Hillary Clinton and teenaged daughter Chelsea by his side.

"We've got a bridge to build and I'm ready if you are," Clinton said in echoing his campaign theme of a bridge to the 21st century. "Today the American people have spoken, they have affirmed our course, they have told us to go forward.
He thanked everyone remotely connected to his campaign effort and, at the end of the list, he thanked Dole and led the crowd in applause "for his lifetime of service."

Still, Clinton's victory had long been forecast by every national pollster and what Democrats were really hoping for was to win back at least one of the houses of Congress and erase the humiliation of a Republican sweep two years ago.
It appeared the voters preferred Washington power to be divided, even if they did credit Clinton for the prosperity and peace cocooning America in 1996.

The Republicans kept the Senate by winning open seats previously held by Democrats in Alabama, Nebraska and President Bill Clinton's home state of Arkansas. That guaranteed them at least 51 seats in the 100-seat chamber.

The House of Representatives was more in doubt but both ABC and CNN television projected it too would remain in Republican hands once all votes were in. The Democrats needed a net gain of 19 seats to erase the Republican edge and the projections were that they would fall short.

That meant Clinton would have to deal with many an old enemy -- including House Speaker Newt Gingrich and arch-conservative Senator Jesse Helms of North Carolina -- in pushing any ambitious second term plans.
It also remained to be seen whether he would achieve his own goal of winning majority popular support, unlike four years ago when he won with 43 percent in a three-way field.
He was on the edge midway through the counting, with 50 percent support to 42 percent for Dole and 8 percent for Reform Party candidate Ross Perot -- a weaker third party challenger this time.
But for Clinton any victory at all was sweet vindication, befitting the political legend of a man who once dubbed himself "The Comeback Kid."

Exactly two years ago he was written off as finished by many in his own party after disgruntled voters tossed his Democrats out of Congress in droves and handed control of both houses to the Republicans for the first time in 40 years.

The message from voters on Tuesday was very different from the discontent they felt then: the country is now on the right track, they told pollsters as they left ballot stations and their personal financial outlook is much rosier.
They did not seem much to care about Dole's insistent message that Clinton is not very honest or trustworthy.
The crushing dimensions of Clinton's victory were apparent early on.

He swept Dole in most of the big prize electoral-vote states, taking away usually Republican Florida and Ohio among others and adding the big industrial states of New York, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Illinois and New Jersey. He capped that later with California, the biggest electoral prize of all with 54 votes.
Dole could retaliate only in Texas and North Carolina from the major states plus a handful of smaller ones.
The tale of Clinton's victory seemed clearly to be of voters rating personal security and national prosperity far above the character issues and tax-cut promises Dole pushed.
ABC News reported 58 percent of those leaving the polls rated the economy in good shape.
That compared with only 19 percent four years ago, when Clinton ousted Republican George Bush by hammering at discontent with a weak economy.

NBC said its exit poll also showed 58 percent believed the country was headed in the right direction, compared to two years ago when 60 percent thought it was on the wrong track and Republicans won Congress.

The ABC exit poll also suggested Dole's scorching attacks on Clinton's character -- virtually the whole focus of the last two weeks of his campaign -- had gained him little ground among voters who said they cared little about that issue.
